name: Sod's Law
statement: If something can go wrong, it will, and at the worst possible time.
statementAccent: and at the worst possible time
meaning: The British near-synonym of Murphy's law, but with a stronger flavour of personal, ironic bad luck striking at the least convenient moment. The name comes from 'sod' as an unlucky person, the hapless 'unlucky sod' to whom misfortune happens, framing bad luck as something aimed at an individual.
mechanism: Folk perception attributes near-malignant intent to inanimate events, as though the universe were out to get you. Rationally it is explained by selective memory and confirmation bias (we vividly recall exceptional failures and forget mundane successes) helped along by the law of truly large numbers, under which rare-seeming coincidences are common across many trials, and by human negativity bias.

examples.text: Toast landing butter-side down is the emblem, and, Robert Matthews argued, partly real: dropped from a typical table height it rotates only about half a turn before it lands, so physics, not superstition, tips it butter-down.
It rains the day you forget your umbrella or just after you wash the car: the classic Sod's-law illustration of misfortune timed for maximum inconvenience, rationally an artefact of selective memory.
The other queue always seems to move faster: statistically likely across several lanes, and remembered only when yours lags, so the impression of being singled out is a trick of attention.

variants.name: Murphy's law
variants.text: The American form, 'anything that can go wrong will go wrong', more neutral and engineering-flavoured, with a firmer documented origin than Sod's law's obscure one.

variants.name: The buttered-toast phenomenon
variants.text: Robert Matthews's tongue-in-cheek but genuine physics of falling toast, which won a 1996 Ig Nobel Prize: the one canonical Sod's-law example with a real deterministic basis.

whyItMatters: It is the British folk face of misfortune, capturing the specifically personal, ironic sense of luck turning against you at the worst moment. It also hosts a rare twist: in the buttered-toast case, what looks like pure superstition turns out to have a real physical cause (a reminder to check whether a 'law of bad luck' hides an ordinary mechanism).

working.text: before concluding events are conspiring, remember that hits are recalled and misses forgotten: the engine behind the felt truth of the law.
the toast case shows some 'bad luck' has a physical cause; check whether an ordinary explanation underlies the pattern before invoking cosmic malice.
taken lightly, 'assume the inconvenient outcome' is a nudge toward contingency, not a literal forecast.

limits: It is a humorous folk adage, not an empirical law, mostly explained by selection and observation bias (remembering hits and forgetting misses) with Dawkins dismissing the idea that events 'know' your wishes. Its precise origin is genuinely obscure and effectively undated, with no established coiner. The one notable exception is buttered toast: Matthews argued it genuinely tends to land butter-side down for mundane physics reasons, so a canonical example of the law has a real deterministic basis rather than being pure bias.
misreadings: It is not evidence that the universe targets the unlucky: the pattern is manufactured by memory and large numbers. Its origin is not documented, so confident claims about a first use or coiner are unwarranted, and its distinction from Murphy's law is mostly regional and tonal, with the 'worst possible time' twist overlapping Finagle's law.
origin: A British colloquialism of obscure, undated origin, used where North America says 'Murphy's law' and named from the 'unlucky sod' to whom misfortune happens. The physicist Robert Matthews later gave its toast example a genuine treatment in 'Tumbling toast, Murphy's Law and the fundamental constants' (European Journal of Physics, 1995), which won a 1996 Ig Nobel Prize.
